text: The name for this mapping differs by provider: Akamai calls it a property (the configuration that controls how edge servers respond to requests), and Amazon CloudFront calls it a distribution.
why: Readers will meet both terms in vendor docs.

text: To use your own hostname (like edge.arpitbhayani.me), you add a DNS CNAME pointing to the CDN's edge hostname. Once the CNAME is in place, Akamai's DNS servers return the IP address of the best Akamai servers for that user.
why: Explains how the custom CDN name in the demo is wired up in DNS.

text: CDNs do not cache every response automatically. Cloudflare, for example, caches by file extension and does not cache HTML or JSON by default, and it skips responses marked Cache-Control private, no-store, no-cache or max-age=0, or carrying a Set-Cookie header. Cache rules or origin headers make other responses eligible.
why: Without this, a learner expects API/JSON responses to be cached and is surprised when they are not.

text: How long the CDN keeps a response is controlled by the origin's Cache-Control max-age (or s-maxage, which applies only to shared caches like CDNs) together with the CDN's minimum/maximum TTL settings. With no cache policy and no header, CloudFront's default TTL is 24 hours.
why: Shows where the TTL in the caching flow actually comes from.

text: Besides waiting for the TTL or invalidating, you can give each new version of a file a new name (e.g. logo.v2.png). CloudFront recommends versioned file names for frequently updated files: they also beat browser and proxy caches and cost nothing to invalidate.
why: A third, often better, way to handle changed content; fits the store-an-ID design.

text: The origin does not have to be on the public internet: since November 2024, CloudFront VPC origins can deliver content from applications in a private VPC subnet.
why: Corrects the 'origin must be public' simplification with a concrete current option.

text: On AWS the native integration is origin access control (OAC): the S3 bucket stays private, its bucket policy allows the CloudFront service principal for one specific distribution, and CloudFront signs every request it sends to S3. No access keys are uploaded to the CDN.
why: Gives the concrete, keyless mechanism behind 'native S3 integration'.

text: S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability and 99.99% availability over a year, storing objects across at least three Availability Zones.
why: Gives the exact figures, a common interview question.

text: On AWS, putting CloudFront in front of S3 also changes the bill: data transfer between CloudFront and AWS origins is waived, so you pay CloudFront delivery rather than S3 egress for the cached traffic.
why: Makes the cost side of the CDN-vs-S3 comparison concrete.

text: As of October 2026, AWS lists two Regions in India (Mumbai and Hyderabad, three Availability Zones each), while its CDN, CloudFront, lists standard edge locations in 7 Indian cities plus embedded PoPs in 46 more.
why: Gives current, sourced numbers for the 'regions vs edge locations' comparison.

text: Per-user prefixes also help throughput: S3 supports at least 3,500 write and 5,500 read requests per second per partitioned prefix, and there is no limit on the number of prefixes in a bucket.
why: Adds a performance reason for the user_id/photo_id layout.

text: In CloudFront, you register public keys in a trusted key group and sign URLs with the matching private key (RSA 2048 or ECDSA 256). The CDN verifies the signature and then checks the expiry in the policy. Adding a query parameter after signing makes the URL fail with HTTP 403.
why: Shows exactly what 'certificate attached so no one can change it' is, and explains the demo's tamper error.

text: The expiry is checked when each request arrives: a download that started just before expiry still completes, but a retry or a Range GET after the expiry time fails.
why: Clarifies that expiry is per request, not tied to cache TTL.

text: Middle-ground options exist between 'pseudo privacy' and no CDN. CloudFront signed URLs can use a custom policy that limits access to the viewer's IP range as well as a short expiry. Signed cookies can protect many files without changing their URLs.
why: Shows that tighter privacy does not force dropping the CDN.

text: Other CDNs offer the same idea under different names. Cloudflare's token authentication checks a URL parameter of the form verify=<timestamp>-<MAC>: it recomputes an HMAC of the path with a shared secret and rejects the request if the MAC differs or the token has expired.
why: Shows that the stateless check works the same way across CDNs.

text: Every distinct parameter combination is a separate cached (and often billed) variant. Cloudflare bills each unique width from width=auto as a separate transformation, so many sites round widths to a few fixed sizes. Cloudflare also warns not to rely on blur to hide content, because anyone can edit URL parameters.
why: A practical cost/cache-hit pitfall of client-chosen widths.

text: Not every CDN has image processing built in. With Amazon CloudFront, AWS provides 'Dynamic Image Transformation for Amazon CloudFront', a solution you deploy in your own account (Lambda or ECS using the sharp library) that CloudFront caches in front of.
why: Sets the right expectation when choosing a CDN for image optimisation.

text: GIPHY serves its GIFs, stickers and clips through Fastly, which handles tens of billions of requests a day, with peaks of about 400,000 requests per second.
why: Gives the scale behind the Giphy example.

text: Netflix runs its own CDN, Open Connect. It places Open Connect Appliances inside ISP networks so that video is served from inside the viewer's ISP.
why: Names the CDN behind the student's Netflix remark.

text: AWS has said publicly that S3 is built on hard disk drives, millions of them, and that HDDs growing in capacity but not in speed shapes S3's design.
why: Confirms the teacher's 'S3 is not on SSDs' point with a primary source.

text: With anycast, many machines share the same IP address, and internet routing sends each user to the nearest one. So a Cloudflare user gets the same IP anywhere in the world but lands on a nearby data center.
why: Explains the BGP part of 'nearest CDN node', separately from DNS.

text: To avoid a burst of requests to the API when the cached hashtag response expires, the origin can send Cache-Control: max-age=N, stale-while-revalidate=M. The CDN then keeps serving the stale copy for up to M seconds while it fetches a fresh one in the background.
why: A standard refinement to plain TTL expiry for hot cached API responses.
